intro: A monk in Thailand walks barefoot at dawn with an alms bowl. A student in Chicago sits in a meditation hall and watches her breath. A family in Kyoto listens to a temple bell ring 108 times on New Year's Eve. A Tibetan monk in exile chants a mantra in India. All four call themselves Buddhists, and all four trace their practice to one teacher who lived in northern India about 2,500 years ago.

This unit studies that teacher and the traditions that grew from him. The first chapter reads the Buddha's life as the tradition tells it, then studies the core teachings that nearly all Buddhists share: the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, the Three Marks of Existence and the Three Jewels, using the Dhammapada in Max Müller's 1881 translation. The second chapter follows the sangha, the community of monks, nuns and laypeople, as it carried the teaching across Asia and into the United States, dividing into Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana along the way.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain the Four Noble Truths in your own words, read a verse of the Dhammapada closely, compare the Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana branches without ranking them, and describe how Buddhism changed as it met new cultures, from China to Chicago. As in every unit, the goal is to understand what Buddhists believe and practice, attributed to them and described fairly, not to decide whether it is true.
bigQuestion: What did the Buddha teach about suffering and its end, and how did that teaching stay recognizable while it changed across Asia and the world?

test.q: According to Buddhist tradition, what four sights led Siddhartha to leave the palace?
choices: An old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering holy man
A king, a soldier, a merchant and a farmer
A tree, a river, a deer and a lotus
His wife, his son, his father and his teacher
test.why: The traditional story says Siddhartha saw age, sickness, death and a renouncer, which set him on his search.

test.q: Why did Siddhartha give up extreme fasting, according to the tradition?
choices: He found that self-torture, like luxury, did not end suffering
The five ascetics told him to stop
test.why: After about six years of severe practice he chose the Middle Way between indulgence and self-torture.

test.q: Which Noble Truth names craving, or tanha, as the cause of suffering?
test.why: The second Noble Truth says suffering arises from craving; the third says it ends when craving ends.

test.q: Right speech, right action and right livelihood belong to which group of the Eightfold Path?
test.why: Teachers group these three as sila, ethical conduct; view and intention are wisdom, and effort, mindfulness and concentration are mental discipline.

test.q: Nagasena compares the self to a chariot. Which of the Three Marks is he teaching?
test.why: The chariot is only a name for its parts, and Nagasena says the word I works the same way, which is the teaching of anatta.

test.q: What does a Buddhist do when taking refuge?
choices: Commits to the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, the Three Jewels
Leaves home to become a monk
test.why: Taking refuge in the Three Jewels is the act that marks many people as Buddhists; it does not require becoming a monk.

test.q: Which translation of the Dhammapada does this course quote, and what should a reader notice about it?
choices: Legge's 1861 version, which uses Chinese terms
Arnold's 1885 version, which is in rhyme
Müller's 1881 version, which uses Victorian words such as sin and church
A modern version that uses only Pali terms

test.q: Which teaching marks a key difference between Buddhism and the Upanishads?
choices: Whether there is an eternal self, or atman
test.why: The Upanishads teach an eternal atman one with Brahman; Buddhists teach anatta, non-self.

test.q: Why is the emperor Ashoka important to Buddhist history?
choices: After the Kalinga war he supported the sangha and sent the teaching abroad
test.why: Ashoka's edicts record his turn to dharma, and his support helped carry Buddhism beyond India, including to Sri Lanka.

test.q: Which scripture is central to Theravada Buddhism?
test.why: Theravada preserves the Pali Canon, with its three baskets of Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma.

test.why: Mahayana is the main branch of East Asia; Theravada is in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia; Vajrayana is in Tibet and nearby lands.

Both practice only the alms round

test.why: Shinran's school stresses trust in Amida's other-power, while Dogen's Soto Zen centers on seated meditation.

test.why: The mandala, a sacred diagram of an awakened world, is a Vajrayana practice that Tibetan monks create in sand.

test.q: Why did some Confucian critics in China object to Buddhist monks?

Monks worshiped Confucius as a god
test.why: Filial piety centers on duty to parents and ancestors; stories such as Mulian's showed monks honoring that duty.

test.q: What happened in Chicago in 1893 that matters to the history of Buddhism in America?

Buddhist speakers such as Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku addressed the World's Parliament of Religions
The Buddhist Churches of America was founded
test.why: At the 1893 Parliament, many Americans heard Buddhists describe their tradition in their own words for the first time.

story.title: Four Sights Beyond the Wall
story.kicker: As Buddhist tradition tells it, a sheltered prince rode out of his palace four times and came back a different man.
paragraphs: The story that Buddhists have told for more than two thousand years begins with a father who wanted to protect his son. According to tradition, a prince named Siddhartha Gautama was born into the Shakya clan in the foothills of the Himalayas, in what is now southern Nepal. A seer is said to have told his father that the boy would become either a great king or a great religious teacher. The father wanted a king. So he built a life for Siddhartha inside high walls, with gardens, music, fine food and no sight of anything sad.

The tradition says the plan worked until Siddhartha was twenty-nine. Then he asked to ride out through the city. On the first ride he saw a man bent with age, his skin loose and his hands shaking. Siddhartha had never seen an old person. His charioteer, Channa, explained that this happens to everyone who lives long enough. On the second ride the prince saw a man burning with fever, too weak to stand. On the third he saw a corpse being carried to the cremation ground, and mourners weeping behind it.

Each time, the story says, the prince asked the same question: does this happen to me too? Each time the answer was yes. Age, sickness and death were not accidents that struck other people. They were the shape of every human life, including his own, including the lives of his wife and his newborn son. The gardens and music now seemed to him like a curtain drawn over a window.

On the fourth ride he saw something different: a wandering holy man with a shaved head and a single robe, carrying a bowl and walking calmly. The man owned nothing, yet he looked at peace. Siddhartha asked who he was. Channa told him this was a renouncer, someone who had left home to search for an end to suffering. That night, the tradition says, the prince slipped out of the palace, cut his hair, exchanged his silk for a plain robe and began the search himself.

Historians cannot confirm the details of this story, and Buddhists themselves read it in different ways. Some take it as history, others as a teaching told in the form of a life. But nearly every Buddhist school agrees on what the four sights mean. Before anyone can look for a cure, they have to admit that something is wrong. The four sights are the moment the diagnosis begins.
story.think: The story says the prince's father tried to hide old age, sickness and death from him. Why might a tradition begin its founder's story with that failure rather than with a miracle?

lessons.title: Siddhartha in History and Tradition
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists trace their tradition to Siddhartha Gautama, a teacher in northern India around the fifth century BCE, whose life is known mostly through later Buddhist texts.
reading: In the town of Lumbini, in southern Nepal, a stone pillar stands in a park. It was raised around 250 BCE by the Indian emperor Ashoka, and its inscription says that the Buddha was born here. It is the oldest physical marker of the Buddha's life that we have. Buddhists from Thailand, Japan, Tibet, Sri Lanka and the United States travel to Lumbini to walk where they believe their teacher's story began.

The man they honor is *Siddhartha Gautama*. Buddhist tradition says he was born a prince of the *Shakya* clan, which is why he is also called Shakyamuni, the sage of the Shakyas. Scholars agree that he was a real teacher who lived in the Ganges valley of northern India. They do not agree on his dates. Older scholarly estimates place his death around 483 BCE, and Sri Lankan tradition earlier still; many historians today prefer a date closer to 400 BCE. This course follows common practice and says he lived in about the fifth century BCE.

Almost everything else we know comes from Buddhist texts written down centuries after his death, first in the *Pali* language and later in Sanskrit and Chinese. These texts were preserved as teaching, not as newspaper reports. That does not make them worthless as history, but it means a student should read them the way this course reads any sacred text: asking who wrote them, for whom, and why. Buddhists themselves hold a range of views, from taking every detail as fact to treating the life story as a pattern that every seeker can follow.

The title *Buddha* is not a name. It comes from a word meaning awake, so Buddha means the awakened one. In Buddhist teaching, Siddhartha became the Buddha at a specific moment, which this section will reach. Until then he was a prince, then a wandering seeker like thousands of others in an India full of new religious movements, including the Jain teacher Mahavira, who lived at about the same time.

lessons.title: Renunciation and the Middle Way
lessons.mainIdea: After years of extreme self-denial nearly killed him, Siddhartha chose a Middle Way between luxury and self-torture, and Buddhists see that choice as the foundation of the path.
reading: A famous statue from Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan, shows a seated man so starved that every rib and vein stands out and his eyes have sunk into his skull. It is a portrait of Siddhartha during the years after he left home. According to tradition, he first studied with two meditation teachers, mastered what they taught, and found it did not end suffering. Then he joined five ascetics in the forest and tried to conquer the body by force.

An *ascetic* is someone who practices severe self-denial for a religious goal, and in ancient India there were many. The texts say Siddhartha ate a single grain of rice a day, held his breath until his head roared, and sat unmoving in the heat and cold. Tradition says that he grew so thin he could feel his spine through his stomach. After about six years he collapsed by a river. A village girl named Sujata offered him a bowl of rice cooked in milk, and he accepted it. His five companions, disgusted, left him.

Buddhists remember that bowl of rice as a turning point. Siddhartha had lived in a palace of pleasure and found it empty. He had lived in a forest of pain and found it useless. The body, he concluded, is the instrument of the search, and a broken instrument cannot play. In his first sermon he would name two extremes to avoid: devotion to sense pleasure and devotion to self-torment. Between them lies what he called the *Middle Way*.

The Middle Way is not a rule about eating. It is a general principle that later Buddhist thinkers applied to almost everything: to how hard to practice, to how to hold opinions, and to how to think about the self. A monk in Thailand today eats one or two meals before noon and none after, which is more than the starving ascetic ate and less than the prince did. Buddhists point to that schedule as the Middle Way made into a daily habit.

words.d: a person who practices severe self-denial, such as fasting or enduring pain, for a religious goal
the Buddha's teaching that the path runs between the extremes of indulgence and self-torture
giving up home, family and possessions to pursue a religious search; the Buddha's departure from the palace

look.title: Two Extremes and a Path
look.text: Picture two rooms. In the first, a prince eats what he likes, sleeps on silk and never hears a sad word. In the second, a starving man sits in the forest, eating a grain of rice a day and holding his breath until he faints. Buddhist tradition says Siddhartha lived in both rooms and left both. The first sermon calls the two rooms two extremes that a seeker should avoid.
look.prompt: Name one modern situation, not about food, where a person might swing between these two extremes. What would a Middle Way look like there?

check.q: In the tradition, what did Sujata's bowl of rice and milk mark?
choices: The start of Siddhartha's six years of fasting
His first meeting with the five ascetics
The moment he became a king
His decision to abandon extreme self-denial
check.why: Accepting the rice ended the years of near starvation; his five companions left him because of it, and the Middle Way followed.

check.q: What two extremes does the Middle Way run between?
check.why: The first sermon names devotion to sense pleasure and devotion to self-torment as the two extremes to avoid.

check.q: What is an ascetic?
choices: A wealthy patron who feeds monks
Someone who practices severe self-denial for a religious goal
A charioteer who serves a prince

lessons.title: Awakening Under the Bodhi Tree
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists believe Siddhartha reached full awakening while meditating at Bodh Gaya, and that he then taught for forty-five years before his death.
reading: At Bodh Gaya, in the Indian state of Bihar, a large fig tree grows beside a stone temple. Pilgrims sit beneath it in silence, and some tie prayer flags to its branches. Buddhists hold that this tree descends from the one under which Siddhartha sat down one evening and vowed not to rise until he understood the cause of suffering. The species is now called the *bodhi* tree, from the word for awakening.

The texts describe that night as a struggle. A figure named *Mara*, whose name means death, tried to break Siddhartha's concentration with armies, storms, temptations and finally doubt. Mara asked who could witness that Siddhartha deserved awakening. In a gesture that appears in countless statues, Siddhartha touched the ground with his right hand and called the earth itself as witness. Buddhists read Mara in different ways: some as a real being, many as a picture of fear and craving inside the mind.

Toward dawn, the tradition says, Siddhartha saw his past lives, saw how beings rise and fall according to their actions, and saw the chain of causes that produces suffering and the way to break it. At that moment he became the Buddha. He is said to have hesitated to teach, thinking no one would understand, and then to have walked to the Deer Park at *Sarnath*, near Varanasi, where he found the five ascetics who had abandoned him. His first sermon to them is called setting the wheel of the teaching in motion.

For the next forty-five years, according to the texts, the Buddha walked the roads of the Ganges valley, teaching kings, farmers, merchants and outcasts, and gathering a community of monks and nuns. He died at about eighty near the town of Kushinagar, after eating a meal that made him ill. His last recorded words, in the Pali account, urge his followers to work out their liberation with diligence because all conditioned things pass away. Buddhists call his passing the *parinirvana*, the final release.

words.d: awakening; the name given to the tree at Bodh Gaya under which Buddhists believe Siddhartha became the Buddha
in Buddhist texts, the tempter whose name means death; he tries to stop the Buddha's awakening and is often read as a figure for fear and craving
the Deer Park near Varanasi where tradition says the Buddha gave his first sermon to the five ascetics
the final release at the Buddha's death, when Buddhists believe he passed beyond rebirth entirely

look.title: The Earth as Witness
look.text: Thousands of Buddha statues show the same pose: seated cross-legged, left hand in the lap, right hand reaching down to touch the ground. The texts say this is the moment Mara demanded a witness and Siddhartha answered by calling on the earth. Some Buddhists understand Mara as a real being; others read him as fear, craving and doubt taking a shape. Either way the answer is the same gesture: not an argument, but a touch.
look.prompt: Why might a tradition choose the ground, rather than a god or a teacher, as the witness at this moment? What does the gesture claim about where authority comes from?

check.q: Where do Buddhists believe Siddhartha reached awakening?
choices: In the Deer Park at Sarnath
Under a tree at Bodh Gaya
check.why: Bodh Gaya is the site of the bodhi tree; Sarnath is where the first sermon was given, and Kushinagar is where he died.

check.q: What does the Buddha's earth-touching gesture answer, according to the texts?
choices: The five ascetics' request for food
Mara's demand for a witness to his right to awaken
His father's demand that he return home
check.why: Mara asked who could witness Siddhartha's worthiness, and he touched the ground to call the earth as witness.

check.q: The Buddha's first sermon is traditionally described as what?
choices: Lighting the lamp of the world
Setting the wheel of the teaching in motion
check.why: The Pali tradition names the first sermon at Sarnath the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching, or dharma.

lessons.title: The First Truth: Dukkha
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha's first truth is that ordinary life is marked by dukkha, a word that covers pain, stress and the unreliability of everything we lean on.
reading: A doctor in an emergency room does not begin with the cure. She begins by asking what hurts. Buddhists often describe the Buddha's first sermon the same way: as a physician's four steps, which name the illness, its cause, whether it can be cured, and the treatment. These are the *Four Noble Truths*, the core of Buddhist teaching in every school. The first is the diagnosis: there is *dukkha*.

Dukkha is a Pali word usually translated as suffering, but that English word is too narrow. Dukkha includes obvious pain, such as sickness, grief and death. It also includes the frustration of not getting what we want and the anxiety of losing what we have. At its deepest, it means that nothing we grasp can be relied on, because everything changes. A good meal ends. A friendship shifts. A body ages. Even happiness carries dukkha, Buddhists say, because it cannot last.

The first sermon lists the forms: birth is dukkha, aging is dukkha, sickness is dukkha, death is dukkha; being joined to what one dislikes, being parted from what one loves, and not getting what one wants are dukkha. Notice that the list is not a claim that life is only misery. Buddhists insist the first truth is not pessimism but honesty, in the way that a diagnosis is not pessimism. Its purpose is to make a cure possible.

Compare this starting point with others in this course. The Hebrew Bible opens with a good creation and asks how it went wrong. The Buddha opens with an observation about experience and asks what drives it. Neither tradition denies pain; they place it differently. A student comparing them should describe each on its own terms rather than deciding which is gloomier or more hopeful.

words.d: the core of the Buddha's teaching: there is suffering, it has a cause, it can end, and there is a path to its end
a Pali word for suffering in the widest sense: pain, frustration and the unreliability of everything that changes
the Buddha's first teaching, given to five former companions at Sarnath, in which he set out the Four Noble Truths

look.title: Reading the Diagnosis
look.text: Two statements: (1) Life is nothing but misery. (2) Everything that arises passes away, and clinging to what passes brings distress. Buddhist teachers say the first truth means the second statement, not the first. Yet many people hear the first when they meet the word suffering.
look.prompt: Explain the difference between the two statements in your own words. Why would translating dukkha simply as suffering make a reader hear statement one?

check.q: Buddhists often compare the Four Noble Truths to which set of steps?
choices: A judge's verdict, sentence and appeal
A physician's diagnosis, cause, prognosis and treatment
A builder's foundation, walls and roof
check.why: The reading presents the truths as a doctor's method: what is wrong, why, whether it can be cured, and how.

check.q: Which best captures the meaning of dukkha?
choices: Suffering in a wide sense, including the unreliability of everything that changes
check.why: Dukkha includes pain, frustration and the fact that nothing we grasp lasts; it is broader than physical pain and is not a punishment.

check.q: How do Buddhist teachers answer the charge that the first truth is pessimistic?
choices: They agree that life is only misery
They say the truth applies only to non-Buddhists
They say suffering is an illusion that does not exist
They say it is an honest diagnosis whose purpose is to make a cure possible
check.why: The reading says the first truth is honesty, not pessimism, like a diagnosis that opens the way to treatment.

lessons.title: Craving and Its Ending
lessons.mainIdea: The second and third truths teach that suffering arises from craving and that when craving ceases, suffering ceases, a state Buddhists call nirvana.
reading: In the Pali texts the Buddha compares the mind to a fire that keeps burning as long as fuel is added. The second Noble Truth names the fuel. Suffering arises from *tanha*, a word that literally means thirst and is usually translated as craving. It is the pull toward pleasant things, the push away from unpleasant ones, and the wish for existence itself to go on as we like. Buddhists say craving is not the same as needing food or wanting a friend to be well. It is the grasping that turns a wish into a demand.

The teaching connects craving to a wider view of cause and effect. Buddhists hold that actions driven by craving, hatred and ignorance produce results, and that beings are reborn again and again in a cycle called *samsara*, carrying the fruits of past action, or *karma*. The word karma means action; in Buddhist usage it points to intentional action and its consequences. Rebirth in Buddhism differs from the Hindu idea in one key way, which a later lesson explains: Buddhists deny a permanent soul that passes from life to life.

The third truth is the good news of the diagnosis. Because suffering has a cause, removing the cause removes the suffering. When craving is extinguished completely, what remains is *nirvana*. The word means blowing out, like a flame. Buddhist teachers are careful to say nirvana is not nothingness and not a heaven; it is the end of greed, hatred and delusion, and with them the end of rebirth. The Buddha is said to have declined to describe it in ordinary terms, and in one parable he compares his teaching to a raft that a traveler leaves behind once he reaches the far shore.

Different Buddhists describe nirvana in different ways. Theravada texts emphasize the peace of the person who has fully let go, called an arhat. Some Mahayana texts speak of nirvana as not separate from this world, once the world is seen rightly. What all agree on is the logic of the truths: if the fire needs fuel, then stop adding fuel and the fire goes out.

words.d: literally thirst; the craving or grasping that the second Noble Truth names as the cause of suffering
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth that Buddhists (and Hindus and Jains) hold that beings pass through
action; in Buddhist teaching, intentional action and the results it produces in this life and future ones
literally blowing out; the end of craving, hatred and delusion, and so the end of suffering and rebirth

look.title: Hatred Does Not End by Hatred
look.text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.
look.cite: Dhammapada, chapter 1, verse 5, translated by F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10, 1881
look.prompt: The second truth says craving and hatred feed suffering. How does this verse turn that diagnosis into practical advice? What would it ask of someone who has been wronged?

check.q: What does the second Noble Truth name as the cause of suffering?
check.why: The second truth teaches that suffering arises from tanha, thirst or craving, the grasping that turns wishes into demands.

check.q: What does the word nirvana literally mean?
choices: Blowing out, as of a flame
check.why: Nirvana means blowing out; Buddhists use it for the extinguishing of craving, hatred and delusion.

check.q: In Buddhist usage, karma most precisely refers to what?
choices: The soul that passes from life to life
check.why: Karma means action; Buddhists use it for intentional action and the results it produces, not for fate or luck.

lessons.title: The Eightfold Path
lessons.mainIdea: The fourth truth is the Eightfold Path, eight linked practices that Buddhists group under wisdom, ethical conduct and mental discipline.
reading: Above the doors of many Buddhist temples, and on their gates and roofs, you will see a wheel with eight spokes. It is the *dharma* wheel, and in Buddhist art its eight spokes stand for the fourth Noble Truth: the *Eightfold Path*. The word dharma has many meanings in India. In Buddhism it means above all the Buddha's teaching, and also the way things truly are. The path is the treatment the physician prescribes.

The eight parts each begin with a word usually translated right, in the sense of complete or skillful rather than correct on a test. They are right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. Buddhists do not treat these as eight steps climbed one after another. They are eight strands of one rope, practiced together, each supporting the others.

Teachers commonly gather the eight into three groups. Right view and right intention are wisdom: understanding the Four Noble Truths and intending kindness and letting go. Right speech, right action and right livelihood are ethical conduct, or *sila*: not lying or speaking harshly, not killing or stealing, and earning a living that does not harm others, such as avoiding trade in weapons or living beings. Right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration are mental discipline, or *samadhi*: training the mind through meditation.

A concrete example: a Buddhist shop owner in Chicago who refuses to sell counterfeit goods is practicing right livelihood and right action. When she notices irritation with a rude customer and lets it pass without a sharp reply, she is practicing right mindfulness and right speech. The path, Buddhists say, is not reserved for monks. Its parts fit an ordinary Tuesday.

words.d: in Buddhism, the Buddha's teaching and the truth it points to; the eight-spoked dharma wheel stands for the Eightfold Path
the fourth Noble Truth: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration
ethical conduct; the group of the path that covers speech, action and livelihood
concentration or mental discipline; the group of the path that covers effort, mindfulness and concentration

look.title: Sorting the Spokes

sections.title: Marks of Existence and the Three Jewels

lessons.title: Impermanence, Suffering, Non-Self
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists teach that all conditioned things share three marks: they are impermanent, unsatisfactory and without a fixed self.
reading: In the Milindapanha, a Pali text compiled around the turn of the common era, a monk named Nagasena is questioned by a Greek king named Menander. Nagasena asks the king to point to his chariot. Is it the wheels? The axle? The pole? The king admits it is none of these parts, yet there is no chariot apart from the parts. Chariot, Nagasena says, is a useful name for the parts working together. And so, he argues, is the word I.

This story illustrates the third of what Buddhists call the *Three Marks of Existence*. The first mark is *anicca*, impermanence: everything that arises from causes will change and pass away. The second is dukkha, already studied: what is impermanent cannot give lasting satisfaction. The third is *anatta*, non-self. Buddhists teach that what we call a self is a flow of five changing bundles, the *five aggregates*: physical form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. No unchanging owner stands behind them.

Here Buddhism parts from the Hindu teaching studied in the previous unit. The Upanishads teach that the true self, atman, is eternal and one with Brahman. The Buddha, according to the Pali texts, declined to affirm any such self. Rebirth still happens, Buddhists say, the way one candle lights another: a process continues, but no unchanging thing passes across. Buddhist schools have debated for centuries how to explain this, and a student should present it as a teaching they hold, not as a puzzle they failed to notice.

The Three Marks are meant to be seen, not merely believed. Buddhist meditators watch a sensation arise and fade, and notice that the wish for it to stay is itself a source of distress. Seeing impermanence directly, they say, loosens grasping. That is why the Dhammapada connects knowing the three marks with the way to purity.

words.d: the Buddhist teaching that all conditioned things are impermanent, unsatisfactory and without a fixed self
impermanence; the first mark, that everything arising from causes changes and passes away
non-self; the teaching that no permanent, unchanging self stands behind the changing parts of a person
form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness; the changing bundles Buddhists say make up a person

look.title: Three Verses, Three Marks
look.text: 'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity. 'All created things are grief and pain,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity. 'All forms are unreal,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity.

look.prompt: Match each verse to one of the Three Marks. Müller's phrase 'becomes passive in pain' is often rendered today as 'turns away from suffering.' How does the translation choice change what you picture?

check.q: What point does Nagasena make with the chariot?
choices: That kings should not ride chariots
That the word self, like the word chariot, names parts working together rather than a separate thing
That the soul is the axle of the body
That Greeks could not understand Buddhism
check.why: Nagasena shows the chariot is not found apart from its parts and applies the same reasoning to the self, illustrating anatta.

check.q: On which point does Buddhist teaching differ sharply from the Upanishads?
choices: Whether there is an eternal self, or atman
check.why: Both traditions accept rebirth, karma and meditation; the Buddha declined to affirm the eternal atman that the Upanishads teach.

check.q: Which word names the mark of impermanence?
check.why: Anicca is impermanence; anatta is non-self, sila is ethical conduct and tanha is craving.

lessons.title: Buddha, Dharma, Sangha
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists express commitment by taking refuge in the Three Jewels, the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, and lay Buddhists undertake five precepts.
reading: In a temple in Sri Lanka, in a meditation hall in Colorado, or in a family shrine room in Vietnam, a Buddhist ceremony often begins with the same short chant, in Pali or in translation: I go to the Buddha for refuge; I go to the dharma for refuge; I go to the sangha for refuge. Repeated three times, this is called *taking refuge*. For many Buddhists it is the act that marks a person as a Buddhist, the way the shahada does for a Muslim.

The three refuges are called the *Three Jewels*. The Buddha is the teacher and the proof that awakening is possible for a human being. The dharma is the teaching itself and the truth it describes. The *sangha* is the community: in its strict sense the order of monks and nuns, and in a broader sense everyone who follows the path. Refuge does not mean asking the Buddha to rescue anyone. Buddhists compare it to trusting a doctor, a medicine and the nurses who help you take it.

Along with refuge, lay Buddhists commonly undertake the *five precepts*: to refrain from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from intoxicants that cloud the mind. These are worded as training commitments a person takes on, not as commands from a god. Monks and nuns take many more rules. On holy days some laypeople keep eight precepts, adding, for example, not eating after noon.

Comparing traditions helps here. The Ten Commandments in Exodus are framed as words spoken by God to a people in covenant. The five precepts are framed as steps a person undertakes to reduce harm and clear the mind. Both forbid killing, stealing and lying. A student writing about them should attribute each to its tradition and describe the different frames rather than asking which list is better.

words.d: the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha; the three refuges of Buddhist commitment
the chant and commitment by which a person places trust in the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha
the Buddhist community; strictly the order of monks and nuns, more broadly all who follow the path
the lay Buddhist commitments to refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech and intoxicants

look.prompt: Müller, writing in 1881, used the words Law and Church for dharma and sangha. What do those English words carry that the Pali words may not? What would you choose instead, and why?

check.q: What are the Three Jewels?
choices: The Buddha, the dharma and the sangha

check.q: In its strict sense, what does the word sangha mean?

check.why: Strictly, the sangha is the monastic order; more broadly it names everyone who follows the path.

lessons.title: Meditation and Mindfulness
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist meditation trains the mind through calm and insight, and its mindfulness practices have also spread into secular medicine and schools.
reading: Before dawn in a monastery in Myanmar, a row of monks sits facing a wall. Each is doing something that looks like nothing: attending to the breath as it enters and leaves the nostrils. When the mind wanders to breakfast or an old argument, the monk notices and returns to the breath. This is *meditation*, the mental discipline part of the Eightfold Path, and Buddhists have practiced forms of it for some 2,500 years.

Buddhist teachers commonly describe two families of practice. *Samatha*, calm, steadies the mind on one object, such as the breath, until it becomes still and clear. *Vipassana*, insight, then uses that clarity to observe experience directly: sensations arising and passing, thoughts appearing without an owner. The goal is to see the Three Marks for oneself. A third widespread practice is *metta*, loving-kindness, in which the meditator deliberately wishes well to herself, to friends, to strangers and finally to enemies.

*Mindfulness* is the seventh part of the path. In the Pali texts it means clear, steady awareness of the body, feelings, mind and mental states as they are, without adding or pushing away. Buddhist schools shape it differently. Zen practitioners in Japan sit in silent zazen; Tibetan practitioners may visualize a buddha in detail; Pure Land Buddhists repeat the name of Amitabha Buddha. Each school would say it is training the mind, and each has its own claims about what the training leads to.

Since the late 1970s, mindfulness practices drawn from Buddhism have been adapted for hospitals, therapy and schools with the religious framework removed, beginning with Jon Kabat-Zinn's stress-reduction program at a medical center in Massachusetts in 1979. Some Buddhists welcome this; others argue that mindfulness without the ethical and philosophical parts of the path is something different. A public-school class may teach breathing exercises; it may study, but not lead, the Buddhist practice from which they came.

words.d: the training of attention and awareness; in Buddhism, the mental-discipline group of the Eightfold Path
calm; meditation that steadies the mind on a single object such as the breath
insight; meditation that observes experience directly in order to see impermanence, suffering and non-self
loving-kindness; a meditation of wishing well to oneself, friends, strangers and enemies
steady, clear awareness of body, feelings and mind as they are; the seventh part of the Eightfold Path

look.title: The Same Practice, Two Rooms
look.text: Room one: a monastery in Thailand. A monk watches his breath for an hour, then chants the refuges and the precepts. Room two: a hospital clinic in Illinois. look.prompt: What is the same in the two rooms and what is different? Why might some Buddhists say room two is not Buddhism, and why might others say that does not matter?

check.q: What is the difference between samatha and vipassana?
choices: Samatha is for monks and vipassana is for laypeople
Samatha steadies the mind on one object; vipassana observes experience to gain insight
Samatha is Zen and vipassana is Pure Land
Samatha is chanting and vipassana is silence
check.why: Samatha means calm and focuses the mind; vipassana means insight and uses that calm to see the Three Marks directly.

check.q: In metta meditation, the practitioner does what?
choices: Deliberately wishes well to herself, friends, strangers and enemies
check.why: Metta means loving-kindness; the practice extends good wishes outward in stages, ending with people one finds difficult.

check.q: What happened in 1979, according to the reading?
choices: A stress-reduction program adapted mindfulness for a medical setting without the religious framework
The first Zen temple opened in America
Mindfulness was added to the Eightfold Path
check.why: Jon Kabat-Zinn's program in Massachusetts in 1979 began the secular medical use of mindfulness practices drawn from Buddhism.

lessons.title: Reading the Dhammapada
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada, a collection of 423 Pali verses, is among the most widely read Buddhist texts, and Müller's 1881 translation made it available in English.
reading: Open the *Dhammapada* and the first verse tells you what kind of book it is: All that we are is the result of what we have thought. The book is not a story of the Buddha's life and not a set of monastic rules. It is a collection of 423 short verses in Pali, arranged in 26 chapters by theme: earnestness, thought, the fool, the wise man, anger, the self, the Buddha. Buddhist tradition attributes the verses to the Buddha himself; historians see a collection assembled over time from sayings preserved in the early community.

The Dhammapada belongs to the *Pali Canon*, the scriptures of Theravada Buddhism, which the next chapter treats in detail. It is among the texts most often memorized by Theravada laypeople in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and among the Buddhist texts most often translated into other languages. The name is usually understood as the path of the dharma or the verses of the dharma. Its style is memorable on purpose: images of flowers, arrows, chariots and water repeat, and many verses come in pairs that contrast the careless person with the careful one.

In 1881 the German-born Oxford scholar F. Max Müller published his English translation as volume 10 of the Sacred Books of the East, a fifty-volume series that brought Asian scriptures into English between 1879 and 1910. Müller was not a Buddhist. His translation is in the public domain and is the version this course quotes. It is accurate for its time but uses Victorian words, such as sin, church and Law, that carry Christian associations. Reading it well means noticing those choices, as the toolkit from the first unit taught.

Because the verses are short, the Dhammapada is a good place to practice reading a sacred text closely. Ask of each verse: what does it describe, what does it ask the reader to do, and which of the teachings in this chapter does it assume? A verse about a wheel following the ox assumes karma; a verse about the safe refuge assumes the Three Jewels. Buddhists read the Dhammapada for guidance, and students may read it to understand what that guidance is.

words.d: a collection of 423 Pali verses in 26 chapters, among the most widely read Buddhist scriptures
the scriptures of Theravada Buddhism, preserved in the Pali language and organized in three collections
a fifty-volume series of English translations of Asian scriptures edited by F. Max Müller, 1879–1910

chapters.title: Sangha, Schools and the Spread of Buddhism
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one teacher's path from northern India become many Buddhist traditions across Asia and the world, and what stayed the same as it traveled?

story.title: Two Bells, One Tradition
story.kicker: On a winter night in Kyoto and a Sunday morning in Chicago, a bell calls Buddhists together, and the two sounds are linked by more than two thousand years of travel.
paragraphs: It is almost midnight on New Year's Eve in Kyoto, Japan. At the temple of Chion-in, a crowd stands in the cold beneath a bronze bell taller than a person. A team of monks in black robes grips ropes tied to a heavy wooden beam. One monk calls out, the team leans back, and the beam swings forward into the bell. A deep sound rolls out over the city and hangs in the air for a long time before it fades.

The monks will strike the bell 108 times, some before midnight and some after. In Japanese Buddhist tradition, the number 108 stands for the many worldly desires and troubles that bind a person to suffering. Each stroke is meant to let one of them go, so that the new year can begin with a clearer mind. Temples across Japan do the same thing on the same night, and millions of people listen in person or on television.

More than 6,000 miles away, on Chicago's North Side, a smaller bell sounds on a Sunday morning. It calls members of a Japanese American Buddhist temple to their weekly service. Many of the families have belonged for generations. Their grandparents and great-grandparents came to Chicago in the 1940s, after the United States government released Japanese Americans from the camps where it had held them during World War II. The service includes chanting and a short talk, and the congregation repeats a phrase in Japanese: Namu Amida Butsu.

Both bells belong to the same family of Buddhism, called Pure Land, which centers on a Buddha named Amida. Yet neither temple looks much like the Deer Park where, as the last chapter told, the Buddha first taught. There were no bronze bells there, no Japanese words and no Sunday services. The teaching had to travel across mountains, deserts and oceans, and it changed with every language and culture it entered.

This chapter follows that journey. It begins with the community the Buddha left behind, then follows an emperor who sent the teaching abroad, and then traces the three great branches that grew from it. Along the way it asks a question scholars and Buddhists both ask: when a tradition changes this much, what holds it together?
story.think: The Kyoto bell and the Chicago bell sound very different, yet both temples call themselves Buddhist. What would you want to know before deciding what the two communities share?

lessons.title: Life in the Monastery
lessons.mainIdea: The sangha of monks and nuns lives by the monastic rules of the Vinaya and depends on laypeople, who give food and support in return for teaching.
reading: Just after sunrise in a town in northern Thailand, a line of monks in orange robes walks barefoot down the street. Each carries a covered bowl. Along the way, laypeople kneel and place rice, fruit and curry in the bowls, and the monks chant a short blessing in return. This is the *alms round*, and it has taken place in Buddhist countries for more than two thousand years. The monks do not ask for anything. They simply walk, and the community decides whether to give.

The alms round shows how the *sangha* works. In the strict sense the sangha is the order of fully ordained monks, called bhikkhus, and nuns, called bhikkhunis. Buddhist tradition says the Buddha founded the order of monks early in his teaching. It also says that his aunt and foster mother, Mahapajapati, asked to be ordained and became the first nun. Monks and nuns own almost nothing, do not marry, and devote their lives to study, meditation and teaching.

Their life is governed by the *Vinaya*, the collection of monastic rules. In the Theravada version, fully ordained monks keep 227 rules and nuns keep more than 300. The rules cover large matters, such as celibacy and not killing, and small ones, such as how to wear a robe and when to eat. Each year, during the rainy season, monks traditionally stay in one monastery for about three months of study and practice. This retreat is called vassa.

The relationship between monks and laypeople is an exchange. Laypeople give *dana*, meaning generosity: food, robes, medicine and support for the monastery. Monks give the teaching, blessings and an example of the path. Buddhists believe giving produces good karma, so the gift benefits the giver as well. In some Theravada countries the line of fully ordained nuns died out centuries ago. Since the 1990s some women have been ordained again, and Buddhists continue to debate whether that ordination is valid.

words.d: the daily walk on which monks receive food from laypeople
the Buddhist community; in the strict sense, the order of monks and nuns
the collection of rules that governs the life of Buddhist monks and nuns
generosity; the giving of food, robes and support to the sangha

lessons.title: Ashoka's Change of Heart
lessons.mainIdea: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka turned to Buddhist teaching after a bloody war and promoted the dharma across his empire and beyond it.
reading: Across India and Pakistan, carved on rocks and on tall polished stone pillars, are more than thirty inscriptions left by one ruler in the third century BCE. They are the *edicts of Ashoka*, and they are among the earliest readable written records in Indian history. One of them, carved on a rock face, contains something rare in any age: an emperor admitting publicly that his own war caused terrible suffering and that he regrets it.

*Ashoka* ruled the Maurya Empire, which covered most of the Indian subcontinent, from about 268 to about 232 BCE. Around 261 BCE he conquered the region of Kalinga, on India's east coast. In his thirteenth rock edict he says that about 150,000 people were carried away, about 100,000 were killed, and many more died. He writes that he felt deep remorse. After the war, according to the edicts, he devoted himself to dharma, which he describes as kindness, truthfulness, generosity and respect for all living beings.

Ashoka's edicts do not demand that anyone become Buddhist. They urge respect among religious groups and praise both Buddhist monks and Brahmin priests. But other inscriptions and Buddhist texts make clear that Ashoka supported the sangha, visited Buddhist holy places, and raised the pillar at Lumbini mentioned in the last chapter. The edicts also say he sent envoys to the Greek kingdoms to the west to share his message of dharma.

Buddhist tradition in Sri Lanka adds that Ashoka's son *Mahinda*, a monk, brought the teaching to the island, and that his daughter Sanghamitta, a nun, carried a branch of the bodhi tree there. Historians accept that Buddhism reached Sri Lanka in Ashoka's time, while treating some details as tradition. Today Ashoka's lion capital from Sarnath is the national emblem of India, and a wheel from his pillars stands at the center of India's flag.

words.d: inscriptions on rocks and pillars in which the emperor Ashoka announced his policies, c. 260–230 BCE
Mauryan emperor of India (ruled c. 268–232 BCE) who supported Buddhism after the Kalinga war
a monk, Ashoka's son according to tradition, credited with bringing Buddhism to Sri Lanka

Afterward he turned to the study and practice of dharma. He feels deep sorrow for the conquest, because conquering a free land brings killing, death and exile to its people.

check.q: What event, according to his own edict, led Ashoka to turn to dharma?
check.why: Rock Edict 13 says Ashoka felt remorse for the killing in the Kalinga war and then devoted himself to dharma.

check.q: What do Ashoka's edicts say about other religious groups?
choices: They should be respected, including Brahmin priests
They should pay a special tax

lessons.title: Routes Out of India
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism traveled out of India by sea to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia and by the Silk Road to China, and from there to Korea, Japan and Tibet.
reading: In a cave near the town of Dunhuang, at the western edge of China, a small side room was sealed up around the year 1000 CE. When it was opened in 1900, it held tens of thousands of scrolls in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit and other languages. Among them is a printed Buddhist text from 868 CE, the Diamond Sutra, the oldest dated printed book known. Dunhuang sat on the *Silk Road*, and its caves show how Buddhism traveled with merchants and monks.

Buddhism spread from India along two main kinds of routes. By sea, monks and traders carried it south to Sri Lanka and east to the lands that are now Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. By land, it crossed the mountains of the northwest into Central Asia and followed the Silk Road caravan routes into China by about the first century CE. From China it reached Korea in the fourth century and Japan in the sixth. Tibet received it from both India and China from the seventh century on.

In India itself, Buddhism slowly declined. By around 1200 CE, after centuries of change and the destruction of great monastic universities such as *Nalanda*, few Buddhist institutions remained. Scholars describe many causes, including competition from Hindu devotional movements, loss of royal support and invasions. Buddhism remained alive in the Himalayan regions. In the twentieth century it grew again in India, especially after 1956, when the reformer B. R. Ambedkar led hundreds of thousands of Dalits to convert.

The result is that most of the world's Buddhists today live far from the Buddha's homeland. Common estimates count about 500 million Buddhists, roughly 7 percent of the world's people. Counting is hard, especially in China and Japan, where many people join in Buddhist rites while also practicing other traditions. The numbers in this lesson are estimates, and scholars warn that they depend on how a survey defines a Buddhist.

words.d: the network of overland trade routes linking China, Central Asia, India and the Mediterranean
a great Buddhist monastic university in northeastern India, active for centuries until about 1200 CE
a Mahayana Buddhist text; a printed copy from 868 CE is the oldest dated printed book known

look.title: Where Many Buddhists Live

look.prompt: Which country has the most Buddhists, and which has the largest share of its own people who are Buddhist? Why are those two different questions?

check.q: Why are the Dunhuang caves important to the history of Buddhism?
choices: They are where the Buddha was born

sections.title: Theravada: The Way of the Elders

lessons.title: The Pali Canon in Sri Lanka
lessons.mainIdea: Theravada Buddhists preserve the Pali Canon, first written down in Sri Lanka, and hold up the arhat who reaches nirvana as the goal of the path.
reading: In the hill city of Kandy, in Sri Lanka, stands the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic. Sri Lankan Buddhists believe it holds a tooth of the Buddha. Each year, in a festival called the Esala Perahera, a casket for the relic is carried through the streets on an elephant, with dancers and drummers around it. For centuries, whoever held the tooth was thought to have the right to rule the island. The festival shows how deeply Buddhism is woven into Sri Lankan life.

Sri Lanka is a center of *Theravada*, a name that means the teaching of the elders. Theravada Buddhists hold that they preserve the Buddha's teaching in its earliest surviving form. Their scripture is the *Pali Canon*, also called the *Tipitaka*, or three baskets. The three are the Vinaya, the monastic rules; the Sutta, the Buddha's discourses; and the Abhidhamma, a detailed analysis of mind and matter. According to Sri Lankan chronicles, monks first wrote the canon down on palm leaves in the first century BCE.

Before that, the teaching was memorized and chanted. Groups of monks specialized in different collections, and they recited together to check one another. That oral method explains why many passages repeat the same phrases. Scholars agree the Pali Canon contains some of the oldest Buddhist material that survives, though it was shaped over time. Other early collections also survive in Chinese translation, and comparing them helps scholars study the earliest teaching.

The ideal figure in Theravada is the *arhat*, a person who has followed the path to its end, extinguished craving and reached nirvana. Theravada teachers say anyone can walk the path, but that monks and nuns have the best conditions for walking it fully. Laypeople support the sangha, keep the precepts, meditate and build good karma. Many hope for a better rebirth in which they can go further. The whole system rests on the Buddha's teaching that each person must walk the path themselves.

the scriptures of Theravada Buddhism, preserved in the Pali language

lessons.title: Theravada in Southeast Asia
lessons.mainIdea: In Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, Theravada shapes daily life through temples, temporary ordination and festivals such as Vesak.
reading: In Myanmar, a boy of about ten rides through his village on a decorated pony, dressed in silk like a prince. Musicians and relatives walk beside him. At the monastery his head is shaved, he puts on a robe, and he becomes a novice monk for a few days or weeks. The ceremony, called shinbyu, retells Siddhartha's journey from palace to renunciation. For many Burmese Buddhist families it is one of the most important days in a son's life.

*Temporary ordination* like this is common across Theravada Southeast Asia. In Thailand many young men have traditionally spent a rainy season as monks before marriage or a career. Families believe the practice earns merit, meaning good karma, for the son and for his parents. It also teaches the basics of the dharma and the discipline of the Vinaya. Afterward the young man returns to lay life, but he has lived the path from the inside.

The *wat*, or temple-monastery, is the center of many villages and city neighborhoods. It usually holds a shrine hall with a Buddha image, living quarters for monks, and often a *stupa*, a dome-shaped monument that holds relics. Laypeople come on the holy days of the lunar calendar to hear teaching and keep the eight precepts. Schools, festivals and community meetings have often taken place in the wat.

The largest festival is *Vesak*, held at the full moon of the lunar month that usually falls in May. Theravada Buddhists remember three events on that one day: the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his final passing. Temples fill with lanterns and candles, and people bring flowers and release caged birds as an act of kindness. The United Nations recognizes the day internationally. Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia often mark these three events on separate dates.

a Buddhist temple-monastery in Thailand, Cambodia and Laos
a dome-shaped monument that holds relics or marks a holy place

lessons.title: The Bodhisattva Path
lessons.mainIdea: Mahayana Buddhists hold up the bodhisattva, who seeks awakening in order to free all beings, and teach that all things are empty of fixed existence.
reading: In temples across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, one of the most beloved figures is a graceful being who holds a vase of pure water. In China she is called *Guanyin*, which means the one who hears the cries of the world. In Japan she is Kannon, and in Sanskrit texts Avalokiteshvara. Buddhists pray to her for help in illness, danger and childbirth. She is not a buddha. She is a *bodhisattva*.

A bodhisattva is a being who has vowed to become a buddha, not for personal release alone but in order to free all living beings from suffering. This ideal is the heart of *Mahayana*, a name that means the great vehicle. Mahayana texts began to appear around the first century BCE and first century CE. Their followers called their path great because it aims to carry everyone across. They sometimes contrasted it with the arhat ideal, which Theravada Buddhists would describe in their own terms.

The central virtues of the bodhisattva are compassion and wisdom. Compassion is the wish that all beings be free of suffering. Wisdom, in Mahayana, is above all insight into *emptiness*, in Sanskrit shunyata. Emptiness does not mean that nothing exists. It means that nothing exists on its own, apart from causes and conditions. The Indian philosopher Nagarjuna, around the second century CE, developed this idea in depth. The Heart Sutra, chanted daily in many East Asian temples, puts it briefly: form is emptiness, and emptiness is form.

Mahayana also produced new scriptures, called sutras, that Mahayana Buddhists regard as the Buddha's teaching. The best known is the Lotus Sutra, which teaches that all beings can become buddhas. One of its parables describes a father who lures his children out of a burning house by promising them carts to play with. Mahayana readers take the burning house as the world of suffering and the carts as teachings suited to each listener.

words.d: the bodhisattva of compassion in China; Kannon in Japan, Avalokiteshvara in Sanskrit
a being who vows to become a buddha in order to free all living beings from suffering
the great vehicle; the Buddhist branch of China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam that centers on the bodhisattva ideal

lessons.title: Pure Land and Amida
lessons.mainIdea: Pure Land Buddhists trust in the vow of Amitabha Buddha and call on his name, hoping for rebirth in his Pure Land, where awakening is assured.
reading: In a Japanese American temple, and in countless homes in Japan, Buddhists repeat a short phrase: Namu Amida Butsu, which means I take refuge in Amida Buddha. The phrase is called the *nembutsu*. Some say it once; some say it thousands of times a day. For some of the largest schools of Japanese Buddhism, this simple act of calling a Buddha's name lies at the center of religious life.

*Amitabha*, called Amida in Japanese, is a buddha described in Mahayana sutras that were popular in China from early on. According to these texts, long ago as a bodhisattva he made a series of vows. One promised that anyone who sincerely called on him would be reborn in his *Pure Land*, a realm of beauty and peace in the west. There, free of the distractions of ordinary life, beings could reach awakening easily. Pure Land practice spread widely in China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan.

In Japan, the monk Honen (1133–1212) taught that in a troubled age most people could not master the difficult practices of monks. They could, however, call on Amida with trust. His follower Shinran (1173–1263) went further. He taught that awakening comes entirely through Amida's power, called other-power, not through one's own effort. For Shinran the nembutsu is an expression of gratitude. He also married, and priests of the school he inspired, Jodo Shinshu, may marry and raise families.

Pure Land shows how varied Buddhism is. A Theravada teacher stresses that each person must walk the path alone; a Shinran follower stresses trust in the power of another. Both call themselves followers of the Buddha, and each can explain from its own texts why its approach fits. A careful student describes both without deciding which is the real Buddhism. Pure Land temples are among the oldest Buddhist congregations in the United States.

the Buddha of Infinite Light, called Amida in Japan, central to Pure Land Buddhism
the realm of Amitabha Buddha, where Pure Land Buddhists hope to be reborn and reach awakening

lessons.title: Zen in Japan
lessons.mainIdea: Zen, which grew from Chinese Chan, emphasizes seated meditation and direct insight, and it shaped Japanese arts from gardens to tea.
reading: At the temple of Ryoanji in Kyoto, visitors sit on a wooden porch facing a rectangle of raked white gravel with fifteen stones set in it. There are no plants except moss, no water and no explanation. The garden is usually dated to the late fifteenth century, and no one knows for certain what it means. Many visitors simply sit and look. The garden is a product of *Zen*, a school of Buddhism that values direct seeing over words.

Zen began in China, where it was called Chan. Both words come from the Sanskrit dhyana, meaning meditation. Chan tradition traces its lineage to Bodhidharma, an Indian monk said to have come to China around the fifth or sixth century; historians treat much of his story as legend. Chan teachers stressed that awakening is not learned from books but seen directly, and that every person already has the nature of a buddha. Chan grew in dialogue with Daoist ideas of naturalness and simplicity.

Zen reached Japan in the late twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The monk Eisai (1141–1215) brought the Rinzai school, which uses the *koan*, a puzzling question or story that a teacher gives a student, such as the question of what one's face was before one's parents were born. The koan cannot be solved by logic, and working on it is meant to break through ordinary thinking. The monk Dogen (1200–1253) founded the Soto school, which centers on *zazen*, simply sitting in meditation, which Dogen treated as awakening itself.

Zen shaped Japanese culture well beyond the temple. The tea ceremony, ink painting, calligraphy, rock gardens and some martial arts all developed under its influence. In the twentieth century, writers such as D. T. Suzuki introduced Zen to American readers, and Zen centers opened in many American cities. Some Zen teachers caution that the art and style are only the surface of Zen. At its core, they say, is the daily discipline of sitting.

in Zen, a puzzling question or story used to push a student beyond ordinary thinking
seated meditation, the central practice of Zen, especially in the Soto school

lessons.title: Vajrayana and the Dalai Lama
lessons.mainIdea: Vajrayana Buddhism, rooted in Tibet, adds mantras, mandalas and teacher lineages to Mahayana, and its best-known figure is the Dalai Lama.
reading: In a school gym or museum hall, four Tibetan monks lean over a wooden platform for days. Using thin metal funnels, they tap out colored sand grain by grain into a detailed circular design of palaces, gates and symbols. When the design is finished, they chant, then sweep it all into a pile and pour the sand into a river. This sand *mandala* has been made in many American cities. The monks say its destruction teaches impermanence.

The mandala belongs to *Vajrayana*, the diamond or thunderbolt vehicle, the form of Buddhism that grew in India and was carried to Tibet from the seventh and eighth centuries CE. Vajrayana accepts the Mahayana bodhisattva ideal and adds practices its followers regard as especially powerful. These include the mandala, a sacred diagram of an awakened world; the *mantra*, a sacred phrase such as Om mani padme hum, linked with the bodhisattva of compassion; and visualization of buddhas in meditation.

Vajrayana stresses the bond between student and teacher. A Tibetan teacher is called a *lama*. Tibetan Buddhists hold that some lamas are reborn again and again to continue their work, and that each rebirth, called a tulku, can be recognized as a child. The most famous line is the *Dalai Lama*, the most prominent teacher of the Gelug school. Tibetan Buddhists regard him as a human form of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

The fourteenth Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, was born in 1935. After China took control of Tibet in the 1950s, he fled to India in 1959, and he has led a Tibetan community in exile from Dharamsala. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989. Tibetan Buddhism is also practiced in Mongolia, Bhutan, Nepal and parts of India and Russia. Questions about Tibet's government and about who will choose the next Dalai Lama remain political as well as religious.

the diamond or thunderbolt vehicle; the form of Buddhism of Tibet, Mongolia and Bhutan
a sacred phrase repeated in practice, such as Om mani padme hum
a teacher in Tibetan Buddhism

lessons.title: Buddhism Meets Confucius and Laozi
lessons.mainIdea: In China, Buddhism met Confucian family values and Daoist ideas, and over centuries the three were described as three teachings that could live side by side.
reading: Every summer, in the seventh lunar month, Chinese families in China, Taiwan, Singapore and overseas communities hold the Ghost Festival. They offer food to ancestors and to wandering spirits, and temples hold services for the dead. The festival is linked to a Buddhist story about a monk named Mulian. He discovers that his mother is suffering in a hell and, on the Buddha's advice, rescues her by making offerings to the sangha.

The story answers a real problem. When Buddhism arrived in China, it met a culture shaped by Confucian teaching, which places *filial piety*, loyalty and care owed to one's parents and ancestors, at the center of a good life. Critics asked how a son could be filial if he shaved his head, left his family and had no children to continue the ancestral rites. The Mulian story shows a monk whose religious life saves his mother. That message made Buddhism fit Chinese family values.

Buddhism also met *Daoism*, the Chinese tradition centered on the Dao, the Way. Early translators sometimes borrowed Daoist words to explain Buddhist ideas; the word dao itself was used for the path. Great translators such as Kumarajiva, around 400 CE, produced Chinese versions of many sutras, and the monk Xuanzang traveled to India and back in the seventh century to collect texts. His journey later inspired the famous Chinese novel Journey to the West.

The meeting was not always peaceful. Some emperors supported Buddhism generously, while others restricted it; in 845 CE the Tang emperor Wuzong closed thousands of monasteries and forced many monks and nuns back to lay life. Over time, however, many Chinese came to speak of the *three teachings*, Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism, as complementary. A family might honor ancestors in Confucian ways, visit a Daoist temple and hold Buddhist funeral rites. The next unit studies Confucianism and Daoism in depth.

lessons.title: Buddhism in America and Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism came to America through Asian immigrants and Western converts, was introduced at Chicago's 1893 Parliament, and today lives in temples across the Chicago area.
reading: In September 1893, at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, a young man from Sri Lanka in a white robe rose to speak. He was *Anagarika Dharmapala*, a Buddhist reformer. Also on the program was Soyen Shaku, a Japanese Zen abbot. For many in the audience it was their first chance to hear Buddhists describe their tradition in their own words. Soyen Shaku's student and translator, D. T. Suzuki, later spent years in America and became one of Zen's best-known writers in English.

By then Buddhism was already in America through immigrants. Chinese workers built temples in California in the 1850s, and Japanese immigrants founded Pure Land temples in Hawaii and on the West Coast; their national organization became the *Buddhist Churches of America*. During World War II the U.S. government forced Japanese Americans on the West Coast into camps. After release, thousands resettled in Chicago, and they founded or strengthened Japanese Buddhist temples on the city's North Side.

A second wave came after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 opened the country to more Asian immigrants. Thai, Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, Korean, Chinese, Tibetan and Sri Lankan Buddhists built temples across the country. The Chicago area now holds dozens of them, from Japanese and Thai temples to Vietnamese, Cambodian and Tibetan centers. Some serve mainly one immigrant community and use its language, while others draw many converts.

Scholars often describe two broad groups among American Buddhists. *Heritage Buddhists* come from families and cultures where Buddhism has long been practiced. Convert Buddhists come from other backgrounds, and many first met Buddhism through meditation. The two groups sometimes practice quite differently, and people debate how they should relate. Surveys suggest that about 1 percent of American adults are Buddhist, while many more practice meditation without calling themselves Buddhist.
